gap: No result ChatGPT got states how tall each extender's screen is next to a 16-inch laptop's own display. A 16-inch 16:10 panel is about 8.5 in tall, against 8.80 in for the 16-inch MacBook Pro's own display, while the Trio 3 Pro's 14-inch wings are about 7.4 in tall (about 1.4 in shorter). The results also never give the number of pixels each setup adds (2 × 16-inch 1920×1200 = 4.61 MP, 3 × = 6.91 MP, Trio 3 Pro 6.27 MP, Duex Float 2 Pro 4.10 MP).
standout_why: I compared against The Office Journal's 16-inch extender page (rank 1 in both chats), WorkCocoon's 16-inch page and iTechGuides' 15-best page (cited in chat 2). None of them works out a pixel count, PPI, screen height or the load on the laptop. The Office Journal and WorkCocoon give only a '1200P' label with no pixel dimensions and no weights. iTechGuides lists 2.9 lb for the Duex Float 2 Pro and calls it 'nearly three pounds' but derives nothing from it. ChatGPT's answers say '15.6–16 inch to match' without saying why in inches.
decides: For a 16-inch laptop, this backs extenders with 16-inch 16:10 panels (FOPO S11, S9G and S788, and the Duex Float 2 Pro stacked above). Their screens come within about 0.3 in of the laptop's own display height. The 14-inch-wing Trio 3 Pro adds more pixels (6.27 MP vs 4.61 MP for a 16-inch dual), but its screens are about 1.4 in shorter and denser (about 189 PPI), and it weighs 4.13 lb (Macworld), 88% of a 4.7 lb MacBook Pro 16. So the Trio is the pick for pixel count, not for a size match. On a 16-inch MacBook Pro M4 Pro (two external displays natively), a dual extender stays within the native limit; the three-screen S788 runs only through FOPO's driver.
